quote: The size and quality of the Haskell community, its breadth and its depth, are both the indicator of Haskell’s success and its cause
what: The size, quality, breadth, and depth of the Haskell community are presented as both the indicator of Haskell's success and its cause.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: It was decided that a committee should be formed to design such a language
what: Haskell was to be designed by a committee formed for that purpose, rather than by an individual.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the paper is supposed to be a history rather than a technical description or a tutorial
what: The authors frame the paper's goal as telling the story (who was involved and what inspired them), a history rather than a technical description or tutorial.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: more widespread use of this class of functional languages was being hampered by the lack of a common language
what: The spread of this class of functional languages was being held back by not having one common language.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: monads and input/output (Section 7)
what: Monads and input/output are named as one of the distinctive areas of the language's evolution.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: providing faster communication of new ideas, a stable foundation for real applications development, and a vehicle through which others would be encouraged to use functional languages
what: The motivation for designing Haskell was the need for a common language, meant to speed communication of new ideas, give a stable foundation for real applications, and draw others to use functional languages.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the nature of the language to be designed (non-strict, purely functional)
what: The language to be designed was fixed as non-strict and purely functional.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: support for programming in the large, such as modules and packages, and the foreign-function interface (Section 8)
what: Support for programming in the large, such as modules, packages, and the foreign-function interface, is identified as a technical area of Haskell.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: there had come into being more than a dozen non-strict, purely functional programming languages, all similar in expressive power and semantic underpinnings
what: By 1987 more than a dozen non-strict, purely functional languages existed, all alike in expressive power and semantic underpinnings; this was framed as an unfortunate situation for the community.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: our account will be skewed towards the meetings and conversations in which we personally participated
what: The authors acknowledge their account will be skewed toward the meetings and conversations they personally took part in, an admitted bias in the record.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the type system, and type classes in particular (Section 6)
what: Among Haskell's technical contributions, the type system and type classes in particular are singled out as distinctive aspects worth reflection.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Algebraic data types were extended in several ways: new-
what: Algebraic data types were extended with newtypes, strictness annotations, and named fields.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the easiest way to move forward was to begin with an existing language, and evolve it in whatever direction suited us.
what: A key outcome of the first meeting was that the easiest way forward was to start from an existing language and evolve it.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: “Cons should not evaluate its arguments”
what: Friedman and Wise framed lazy evaluation from a Lisp perspective with the slogan that cons should not evaluate its arguments.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: we intended the language to be quite conservative, rather than to break new ground
what: The committee intended a conservative language that embodied the current consensus of ideas and united the disparate groups, rather than breaking new ground.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Type classes were generalised to higher kinds—so-called “constructor classes”
what: Type classes were generalised to higher kinds, giving constructor classes.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Haskell owes a considerable debt to Miranda, both for general inspiration and specific language elements that we freely adopted
what: Despite the fork, Haskell owes Miranda a considerable debt, in general inspiration and in specific elements freely adopted where they fit.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: it allowed us the freedom to contemplate more radical approaches to many aspects of the language design. For example, if we had started from Miranda it seems unlikely that we would have developed type classes
what: Not starting from Miranda forced a full new design but allowed more radical approaches; type classes would likely not have been developed from a Miranda base.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the entire text could still be available online and be freely usable in that form by anyone
what: Publishing the Report as a book while keeping the full text freely available online defused a tricky debate about freedom and intellectual property.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: which positioned functional programming as a radical attack on the whole programming enterprise, from hardware architecture upwards
what: Backus's Turing Award lecture recast functional programming as a radical attack on the whole programming enterprise, moving it from mathematical curiosity to practical tool.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the influential development of the Gmachine, which showed that one could compile lazy functional programs to rather efficient code
what: The G-machine showed lazy functional programs could be compiled to efficient code, overturning the assumption that laziness meant graph reduction and graph reduction meant interpretation.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: We abandoned the idea of basing Haskell explicitly on OL very early; we violated the goal of embodying only well-tried ideas, notably by the inclusion of type classes; and we never developed a formal semantics.
what: Several initial goals were not met: the OL basis was abandoned early, the well-tried-ideas goal was violated (notably by type classes), and no formal semantics was ever developed.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: a variety of techniques based on graph reduction were being explored, and in particular Turner’s inspirationally elegant use of SK combinators
what: Lazy languages were implemented through graph reduction techniques, notably Turner's elegant use of SK combinators derived from combinatory calculus.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: many of the features in C# were pioneered by Haskell and other functional languages, notably polymorphic types and LINQ
what: Features of C# were pioneered by Haskell and other functional languages, with LINQ directly inspired by Haskell's monad comprehensions (reported via Erik Meijer).
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: this was a very significant moment because it represented a commitment to stability.
what: The Haskell 98 Report represented a deliberate commitment to stability.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Hope, the language that introduced algebraic data types
what: Hope introduced algebraic data types.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: identified the fundamental importance of the lambda calculus for modelling programming languages
what: Landin and Strachey established the lambda calculus as fundamental for modelling programming languages, grounding both operational and denotational semantics.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Language design is a slow process!
what: The four years taken to shake down Haskell 98 illustrate that language design is a slow process.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Lazy evaluation—with its direct connection to the pure, call-by-name lambda calculus, the remarkable possibility of representing and manipulating infinite data structures, and addictively simple and beautiful implementation techniques—was like a drug.
what: The appeal of lazy evaluation lay in its direct connection to the call-by-name lambda calculus, the possibility of infinite data structures, and simple, beautiful implementation techniques.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Lazy evaluation appears to have been invented independently three times.
what: Lazy (non-strict, call-by-need) evaluation emerged independently three times, igniting interest in lazy functional languages for serious programs.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Turner showed the elegance of programming with lazy evaluation, and in particular the use of lazy lists to emulate many kinds of behaviours
what: Turner demonstrated the elegance of programming with lazy evaluation, using lazy lists to emulate many kinds of behaviours.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: A Library Report was added, reflecting the fact that pro-
what: Haskell 1.3 added a Library Report, recognising that programs can hardly be portable without standard libraries to rely on.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: list comprehensions were generalised to arbitrary monads, a decision that was reversed two years later.
what: Haskell 1.4 generalised list comprehensions to arbitrary monads, a decision reversed two years later (reverted to just lists in Haskell 98).
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: David Turner’s Miranda was by far the most mature. It was pure, well designed, fulfilled many of our goals
what: Of the lazy languages, Miranda was the most mature (pure, well designed, robustly implemented, widely deployed), making it the natural starting-point candidate.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Miranda added strong polymorphic typing and type inference, ideas that had proven very successful in ML.
what: Where SASL and KRC were untyped, Miranda added strong polymorphic typing and type inference, ideas proven successful in ML.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: a small but important moment in any language’s evolution is the moment it is named
what: The authors treat the moment a language is named as a small but important moment in its evolution.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Monadic I/O made its first appearance, including “do” syn-
what: Haskell 1.3 introduced monadic I/O with "do" syntax, dropping the earlier I/O semantics in the Appendix.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the possibility that all this would lead to a radically different non-von Neumann hardware architectures
what: A hope was that lazy evaluation would lead to radically different non-von Neumann hardware; much of this work later proved a dead end when stock-architecture compilers outperformed specialised machines.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: OL will be the default if no clearly better solution exists.
what: The committee process used OL's design as the described default, to be kept for any topic lacking a clearly better solution.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Decisions were no longer limited to a small committee; now anyone reading the Haskell mailing list could participate.
what: After the committee ceased, decisions were no longer limited to a small group; anyone on the mailing list could participate, with Peyton Jones as editor of linguistic minutiae.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Members of the committee became increasingly uncomfortable with the “us-and-them” overtones of having both public and private mailing lists
what: Discomfort with the "us-and-them" of having both public and private mailing lists led debate to move fully public, though decisions were still made by the committee.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: SASL was even used at Burroughs to develop an entire operating system—almost certainly the first exercise of pure, lazy, functional programming “in the large”.
what: SASL was used at Burroughs to build an entire operating system, likely the first exercise of pure, lazy, functional programming at large scale.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: a pure higher-order functional language with lexically scoped variables
what: Turner's SASL was a pure higher-order functional language, a sugared lambda calculus with lexical scoping, that brought Burstall and Darlington's pattern matching into an executable language.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: reasoning that it seemed to be much easier to simulate call-by-name in a call-by-value language (using lambda-expressions as thunks) than to simulate call-by-value in a call-by-name language
what: Reported from an anonymous reviewer: Sussman and Steele kept Scheme call-by-value, reasoning that simulating call-by-name in a call-by-value language (via thunks) is easier than the reverse.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: we felt that they were all roughly the same, bar the syntax, and we started to wonder why we didn’t have a single, common language that we could all benefit from.
what: The many single-site lazy languages were felt to be roughly the same bar syntax, prompting the wish for a single, common language all could benefit from.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

open: whether a shared standard or open extensibility was the better path was left as a genuine difference in goals, not resolved.
quote: we sought the freedom for anyone to extend or modify the language, and to build and distribute an implementation. Turner, by contrast, was strongly committed to maintaining a single language standard
what: Turner declined to let Miranda be the basis: the committee wanted freedom for anyone to extend, modify and distribute the language, while Turner was committed to a single portable standard with no dialects.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: In the end, we abandoned the underlying assumption, and provided full syntactic support for both styles.
what: An underlying assumption that there should be "just one way to do something" (making let and where redundant) was abandoned; full support for both styles was provided and is now regarded as a strength, its extra complexity superficial and explained by syntactic transformations.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the backslash was the closest single ASCII character to the Greek letter λ. However, "->" was used instead of a period in order to reserve the period for function composition.
what: The `\x -> exp` syntax for anonymous functions was chosen to resemble lambda, with backslash as the closest ASCII to λ, and `->` used instead of a period so the period could be reserved for function composition.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Function application is denoted by juxtaposition and associates to the left. Thus, f x y is parsed (f x) y.
what: Function application is denoted by juxtaposition and associates to the left, so `f x y` parses as `(f x) y`, leading to concise and powerful code.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

open: Whether @-patterns binding tightly was a mistake is stated as probable, not settled.
quote: Sadly, this simple rule is not adhered to by @-patterns, which bind more tightly than anything; this was probably a mistake
what: The simple binding rule is not followed by @-patterns, which bind more tightly than anything; this was probably a mistake, though not a major problem given their limited use.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the feeling of the Haskell Committee was that we should avoid the semicolon and its sequential, imperative baggage.
what: Because a language without side effects has no notion of sequencing, the committee chose to avoid the semicolon and its imperative baggage, while still separating declarations.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Our simple solution was to enclose a function identifier in backquotes. For example, x 'f' y is the same as f x y.
what: Having converted infix operators into values via sections, the committee added the reverse: enclosing a function identifier in backquotes makes it infix, as in `x \`elem\` xs`, valued for generality and readability; Miranda used a similar `$elem` notation from PAL.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

open: The choice of `:` for cons and `::` for type signatures is described as remaining controversial to this day.
quote: We adopted from Miranda the convention that data constructors are capitalised while variables are not, and added a similar convention for infix constructors, which in Haskell must start with a colon.
what: From Miranda, data constructors are capitalised and variables are not; infix constructors must start with a colon, chosen for consistency with using single colon `:` for list cons, with `::` for type signatures, a choice opposite to ML and still controversial.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Influenced by these constraints and a desire to "do what the programmer expects", Haskell evolved a fairly complex layout rule
what: Driven by the constraints and a desire to do what the programmer expects, Haskell evolved a fairly complex layout rule, complex enough to be formally specified first in the Haskell 98 Report, yet most users adopt a conforming style.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

open: The reason for their greater popularity in lazy languages is left unexplained ("For some reason").
quote: list comprehensions seem to be more popular in lazy languages; for example they are found in Miranda and Haskell, but not in SML or Scheme.
what: For some reason list comprehensions seem more popular in lazy languages, found in Miranda and Haskell but not SML or Scheme, though present in Erlang and later added to Python and planned for Javascript.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Haskell, like many other languages based on lambda calculus, supports both curried and uncurried definitions:
what: Like other lambda-calculus-based languages, Haskell supports both curried and uncurried definitions.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: a function of two arguments may be represented as a function of one argument that itself returns a function of one argument.
what: Following a tradition from Frege, honed by Schönfinkel and Curry, a function of two arguments is represented as a one-argument function returning a one-argument function; one advantage is that curried form is often more compact.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: there were two different styles in which functional programs could be written: "declaration style" and "expression style".
what: Two styles of writing functional programs emerged: declaration style (multiple equations with pattern matching and guards, where clauses, arguments on the left) and expression style (composing expressions, with let, lambda, case, if).
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Haskell has 21 reserved keywords that cannot be used as names for values or types... keeping it low was a priority of the Haskell Committee.
what: Keeping the number of reserved keywords low (21, against higher counts in other languages) was a priority, and the committee tried to avoid keywords like "as" that might be useful variable names.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: there was also the feeling that all values in Haskell should be "first class"—especially functions.
what: The feeling that all values, especially functions, should be first class clashed with infix operators not being first class, a problem made apparent by the ambiguity of `f + x`.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: we moved them to the left-hand side of the definition... which had the added benefit of placing the guard right next to the patterns on formal parameters... and in a place more suggestive of the evaluation order
what: Where Miranda placed guards on the far right of equations resembling mathematics, Haskell moved them to the left-hand side, better for long definitions, placing the guard next to the patterns and in a place suggestive of evaluation order, viewed as an improvement over mathematical notation.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: one of the most pleasing consequences of our effort has been comments heard... that "Haskell is a pretty language."
what: A pleasing, though not explicit, consequence of the effort on syntax is the repeated comment that Haskell programs look nice.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: the former always binds less tightly than the latter. Thus f x + g y never needs parentheses, regardless of what infix operator is used.
what: Infix application always binds less tightly than conventional function application, so expressions like `f x + g y` never need parentheses; this decision proved good for readability.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: The Haskell Committee wanted expressions to look as much like mathematics as possible, and thus from day one we bought into the idea that Haskell would have infix operators.
what: Wanting expressions to look like mathematics, the committee adopted infix operators from day one, in contrast to Scheme's consistent prefix application.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Exploiting the physical layout of the program text is a simple and elegant way to avoid syntactic clutter.
what: Exploiting the physical layout of the program, via the offside rule, is a simple and elegant way to avoid syntactic clutter; the idea was familiar from SASL and Miranda and goes back to CPL and ISWIM.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: We ended up with a design that differed from our most immediate inspiration, Miranda, in supporting larger function definitions with less enforced indentation.
what: The layout rules had to be very simple, and after exploring variations the committee adopted a design more lenient than Miranda's, supporting larger function definitions with less enforced indentation, because programmers would want large definitions and layout shouldn't get in the way.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: List comprehensions provide a very convenient notation for maps, filters, and Cartesian products.
what: List comprehensions give a convenient notation for maps, filters, and Cartesian products; first suggested by Darlington, popularised and generalised to lazy lists by Turner in KRC as "ZF expression", and named "list comprehension" by Wadler.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: proposed reversing the usual comment convention: lines of code, rather than lines of comment, should be the ones requiring a special mark.
what: Haskell added literate comments (from OL, suggested by Bird, inspired by Knuth's literate programming): reversing the usual convention so code lines carry a special mark, a `>` ("Bird tracks"), with a later Latex-style form marking code by `\begin{code}` and `\end{code}` so one file serves as both typeset paper and program.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: There are lots of ways to define functions in Haskell...but the ways are simple and all fit together in a sensible manner.
what: Haskell offers many ways to define functions, but they are simple and all fit together sensibly.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: what is the meaning of (-42)? The answer is negative 42!
what: Sections introduced an ambiguity around negation: `(-42)` means negative 42, so one must write `\x-> x-42` or `(subtract 42)`; this was viewed as a problem with prefix operators rather than sections, and the committee chose not to buck convention on negation.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: we carefully defined a set of lexemes for each namespace that were orthogonal when they needed to be, and overlapped when context was sufficient to distinguish their meaning.
what: Namespaces were defined to give users freedom while avoiding ambiguity: lexemes orthogonal when they needed to be and overlapping when context was sufficient, so a capitalised name like `Foo` can refer to type constructor, data constructor, and module at once.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: The Haskell Committee in fact did not want any prefix operators, but we couldn't bring ourselves to force users to write something like minus 42 or ~42 for the more conventional -42.
what: Haskell has only one prefix operator, arithmetic negation; the committee wanted none but couldn't force users to write `minus 42` or `~42` instead of `-42`, and the scarcity of prefix operators makes parsing easier.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: we expected people to write programs that generated Haskell programs, and we thought it would be easier to generate explicit separators than layout.
what: Like Miranda, Haskell lets the user override implicit layout with explicit curly braces and semicolons, thought important because people were expected to write programs that generate Haskell programs, for which explicit separators are easier to generate than layout.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: A section is a partial application of an infix operator to no arguments, the left argument, or the right argument—and by surrounding the result in parentheses, one then has a first-class functional value.
what: The solution was a generalised notion of sections (from Wile's dissertation, via IFIP WG2.1 to Bird and Turner/Miranda): a partial application of an infix operator that, parenthesised, yields a first-class functional value, consistent with partial application of curried functions.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: outlawing shadowing is inconsistent with alpha renaming... So, in the end, Haskell allowed shadowing.
what: A minority argued against allowing variable shadowing to avoid accidental capture, but outlawing it is inconsistent with alpha renaming, so in the end Haskell allowed shadowing.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: We also found that syntax, being the user interface of a language, could become very personal.
what: Syntax is the user interface of a language and can become very personal, which is why some of the committee's most heated debates were over syntax.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Despite this, the Haskell Committee worked very hard...on designing (and arguing about) the syntax of Haskell.
what: Against the common view that syntax is trivial and semantics is where the real work lies, the Haskell Committee worked very hard on designing the syntax.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: The longer form was designed to make it easy to comment out segments of code, including code containing comments.
what: Haskell originally supported two comment styles, short comments with `--` to newline and longer nestable comments with `{-` and `-}`, the longer form designed to make it easy to comment out code, including code containing comments.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: It was also important to us that infix operators be definable by the user, including declarations of precedence and associativity.
what: It was important that infix operators be definable by the user, including declarations of precedence and associativity.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: semantics is discussed half as much as syntax, syntax is discussed half as much as lexical syntax, and lexical syntax is discussed half as much as the syntax of comments.
what: Wadler's law describes how committee effort was allotted: semantics discussed half as much as syntax, syntax half as much as lexical syntax, lexical syntax half as much as the syntax of comments, an exaggeration that still reflected strong views on low-level details.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: a where clause is attached to a declaration, not an expression, and scopes over the guards as well as the right-hand sides of the declarations.
what: Adopted from Miranda, a where clause is attached to a declaration (not an expression) and scopes over the guards as well as the right-hand sides; its bindings are lazy, so a binding used in only one clause is fine.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: The most important point is that Haskell's solution allows one to give a different instance to a type-class for the abstract type than for its representation ... It was unclear to us how to achieve this effect with abstype.
what: The most important point is that Haskell's approach allows a different type-class instance for the abstract type than for its representation, which it was unclear how to do with abstype.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Haskell's solution is somewhat cluttered by the Stk constructors, but in exchange an extra construct is avoided, and the types of the operations can be inferred if desired.
what: Haskell's solution is cluttered by the extra constructor but avoids an extra construct and lets operation types be inferred.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: In Haskell, instead of a special construct, the module system is used to support data abstraction. One constructs an abstract data type by introducing an algebraic type, and then exporting the type but hiding its constructors.
what: Instead of Miranda's special abstype construct, Haskell uses the module system for data abstraction: declare an algebraic type, export the type but hide its constructors.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Algebraic types as a programming language feature first appeared in Burstall's NPL ... They were absent from the original ML ... and KRC ..., but appeared in their successors Standard ML ... and Miranda ... Equations with conditional guards were introduced by Turner in KRC
what: Algebraic types first appeared in Burstall's NPL and Hope, were absent from original ML and KRC, and appeared in their successors Standard ML and Miranda; conditional guards came from Turner's KRC.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: The inclusion of basic algebraic types was straightforward, but interesting issues arose for pattern matching, abstract types, tuples, new types, records, n+k patterns, and views.
what: Including basic algebraic types was easy, but pattern matching, abstract types, tuples, newtypes, records, n+k patterns and views raised interesting issues.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: An expression that diverges (or calls Haskell's error function) is considered to have the value 'bottom', usually written ⊥, a value that belongs to every type.
what: An expression that diverges or calls error has the value "bottom" (⊥), a value belonging to every type.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Haskell further extended this rule to apply to type constructors ... and type variables ... This uniform rule was unusual.
what: Haskell extended the capitalization rule to type constructors and type variables, an unusual uniform rule that differed from Standard ML's tick and Miranda's asterisks.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Haskell also took from Miranda the rule that constructor names always begin with a capital, making it easy to distinguish constructors ... from variables ... In Standard ML, it is common to use lower case for both
what: Haskell took from Miranda the rule that constructor names begin with a capital, making constructors easy to distinguish from variables, unlike Standard ML's lower case for both.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Data constructors can be used both in pattern-matching, to decompose a value of Maybe type, and in an expression, to build a value of Maybe type.
what: Data constructors serve both in pattern matching to decompose a value and in expressions to build a value.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

quote: Data types and pattern matching are fundamental to most modern functional languages (with the notable exception of Scheme).
what: Data types and pattern matching are fundamental to most modern functional languages, Scheme being a notable exception.
who: Paul Hudak, John Hughes, Simon Peyton Jones, Philip Wadler

open: whether an empty type should be permitted was left unresolved at the time.

quote: Arrows are an abstract view of computation with the same flavour as monads, but in a more general setting.

quote: Underlying all these developments is the realisation that being explicit about effects is extremely useful, and this is something that we believe may ultimately be seen as one of Haskell’s main impacts on mainstream programming
what: Underlying all these developments is the realisation that being explicit about effects is extremely useful, which the authors believe may be one of Haskell's main impacts on mainstream programming; transactional memory is an example, since the crude IO effect system means most memory operations need not be logged, and transposing STM into Haskell revealed two new composition operators (retry and orElse).

quote: The IO monad provides a way to achieve this goal without giving up the simple, deterministic semantics of purely functional code

quote: it is also possible to implement the IO monad in a completely different style, without any recourse to a stream of requests and responses.
what: Haskell's I/O is specified monadically and can be implemented with continuations (FailCont -> SuccCont a -> Behaviour) or, in GHC, with a world-passing type World -> (a, World), where a dummy token ensures sequencing under lazy evaluation and real side effects are performed.

quote: the Haskell Committee decided quite late in the design process to change the precedence rules for lambda in the context of infix operators
what: To avoid the piling up of parentheses when lambdas nest in the continuation style, the committee changed, late in the design, the precedence rules for lambda in the context of infix operators, letting continuation code look strikingly like the monadic code.

quote: Moggi used monads to modularise the structure of a denotational semantics, systematising the treatment of diverse features such as state and exceptions.

quote: A monad is a kind of “programming pattern”. It turned out that this pattern can be directly expressed in Haskell, using a type class

quote: A monad consists of a type constructor M and a pair of functions, return and >>= (sometimes pronounced “bind”).
what: A monad is a type constructor M together with return and >>= (bind); M a is read as a computation returning a value of type a and perhaps performing side effects, and bind sequences such computations.

quote: There are three laws that these definitions should satisfy in order to be a true monad ... These laws guarantee that composition of functions with side effects is associative and has an identity

open: How to make monads compose modularly is stated as still open.

quote: The key idea is to treat a value of type IO a as a “computation” that, when performed, might perform input and output before delivering a value of type a.

quote: The monadic approach rapidly dominated earlier models. The types are more compact, and more informative.
what: The monadic approach dominated earlier models because the types are more compact and informative, uncluttered by passed continuations, showing the result type, and allowing polymorphic IO types that a fixed Request/Response type could not express.

quote: monads are one of the most distinctive language design features in Haskell. Monads were not in the original Haskell design, because when Haskell was born a “monad” was an obscure feature of category theory whose implications for programming were largely unrecognised.

quote: This happy conjunction of monads and type classes gave the two a symbiotic relationship: each made the other much more attractive.

quote: monads give quite a bit of freedom in how one defines the operators return and >>=, while ML fixes a single built-in notion of computation and sequencing.

quote: The Haskell Committee was resolute in its decision to keep the language pure—meaning no side effects— so the design of the I/O system was an important issue.

quote: An exciting and entirely unexpected development was Launchbury and Peyton Jones’s discovery that imperative computations could be securely encapsulated inside a pure function.
what: An unexpected development was that imperative computations could be securely encapsulated inside a pure function: a state monad parameterised by a type s that infects its references, encapsulated by runST with a rank-2 type, with parametricity ensuring no references leak between encapsulated computations.

quote: Software transactional memory is a recent and apparently very promising new approach to this problem, and one that fits particularly beautifully into Haskell

quote: Most users preferred the do-notation, and generalising comprehensions to monads meant that errors in ordinary list comprehensions could be difficult for novices to understand, so monad comprehensions were removed in Haskell 98.
what: Two syntactic sugars appeared at different times: Haskell 1.3's do-notation (from Launchbury's work) and Haskell 1.4's monad comprehensions; comprehensions were proposed first, yet users preferred do-notation and generalising comprehensions confused novices, so comprehensions were removed in Haskell 98.

quote: unlike runST, which safely encapsulates an imperative computation, there is no safe way to escape from the IO monad.
what: Unlike runST there is no safe way to escape the IO monad, yet all implementations provide unsafePerformIO; its use is a programmer's promise that the I/O's repetition and ordering do not matter, and it can even subvert the type system, so it arguably deserves a longer name.

quote: Here are a few examples of the notions of side effects that one can define with monads:
